newsitem.title: FRANCE: Juppe pledges governments will run policy after EMU.
newsitem.headline: Juppe pledges governments will run policy after EMU.

text.p: French Prime Minister Alain Juppe, marking a difference with Germany, said on Wednesday that governments, and not just the future European Central Bank, must decide economic policy under a single currency.
He also challenged Bonn's proposals for a tough budgetary stability pact to curb government spending after monetary union.

"We will not submit either to numerical norms accompanied by rigid and automatic sanctions, nor to the central bank alone, whose independence we must respect in that it aims to guarantee price stability, but which cannot be a substitute for political authorities," he told parliament in a debate on European policy.
"The euro is above all a political issue. It is not a plaything for central bank governors," Juppe said.
Germany has insisted that countries be fined automatically if they run up excessive budget deficits unless they can prove exceptional circumstances such as severe recession.

Its insistence on putting figures on these exceptions is opposed by virtually all its European partners, and has irked some politicians in France who accuse Bonn of throwing its weight around to impose an "austerity pact".

Juppe insisted the Franco-German alliance, the driving force behind monetary union, was working well. He said he was against changing the franc-mark parity, seen by many as the symbol of Paris' and Bonn's commitment to work together politically.
"Objectively unjustifiable, decoupling the franc would be politically dangerous and...open the way to all those who are hostile to the switch to the European currency," he said.
A week ago, ex-president Valery Giscard d'Estaing called for a sharp depreciation of the franc to boost growth and jobs, a view he reaffirmed in the National Assembly on Wednesday.
His call revived a debate about the merits of monetary union and struck a chord among those who fear a Europe run by a tough inflation-fighting central bank like the German Bundesbank.

Former European Commission head Jacques Delors added his voice to the debate on Wednesday, accusing German leaders of reducing monetary union to the sole issue of deficit-cutting at the risk of stifling growth and jobs.

"The best proof is the very concept of a stability pact proposed by (German Finance Minister Theo) Waigel. It is limited to controlling public deficits and punishing those countries which do not respect the criteria," Delors said in a "letter to a German friend" published by the weekly Le Nouvel Observateur.

The debate in France mirrored one in Germany, where the Social Democratic opposition told Chancellor Helmut Kohl on Wednesday that Europe needed not a stability pact for fiscal discipline but a pact for growth and jobs.
Juppe promised "clarifications" on France's view that elected governments and parliaments must decide on economic, monetary and budget policy.
France's call for a council of ministers to oversee policy under monetary union has so far won little support in the EU.
Juppe also repeated France's view that the dollar was undervalued and said Paris would press its case with its partners in the Group of Seven rich nations.
Despite a proliferation of debate on Europe, there is little sign that opponents of monetary union or of the franc-mark link are gaining the upper hand in France.
An opinion poll published by daily Le Figaro on Wednesday said a majority of French people disagreed with Giscard d'Estaing's call for a weaker franc.
The Ipsos poll found that 46 percent thought the strong franc policy was good for the economy, while 32 percent thought the opposite and 22 percent had no opinion.
